claim: The rapid evolution of a trait in a clade of organisms can be explained by the sustained action of natural selection.
source: The rapid evolution of a trait in a clade of organisms can be explained by the sustained action of natural selection or by a high mutational variance, that is the propensity to change under spontaneous mutation.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: The rapid evolution of a trait in a clade of organisms can be explained by a high mutational variance.
source: The rapid evolution of a trait in a clade of organisms can be explained by the sustained action of natural selection or by a high mutational variance, that is the propensity to change under spontaneous mutation.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: P3.p is the fastest evolving cell fate among vulva precursor cells in Caenorhabditis nematodes.
source: Here, we report on the fastest evolving cell fate among vulva precursor cells in Caenorhabditis nematodes, that of P3.p.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Delattre and Félix, 2001; Kiontke et al., 2007; Braendle et al., 2010; Pénigault and Félix, 2011a) mentioned later in the text.

claim: The causal mutations underlying P3.p's high mutational variance are scattered across the genome.
source: We find that these positions do not present any characteristics of a high mutation rate, are scattered across the genome and the corresponding genes belong to distinct biological pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic mapping data showing mutations on different chromosomes (Figure 3).

claim: The causal mutations underlying P3.p's high mutational variance do not present characteristics of a high mutation rate.
source: We find that these positions do not present any characteristics of a high mutation rate, are scattered across the genome and the corresponding genes belong to distinct biological pathways.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of mutation types, GC content, repeat content, and comparison with other mutation datasets (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: The genes corresponding to causal mutations belong to distinct biological pathways.
source: We find that these positions do not present any characteristics of a high mutation rate, are scattered across the genome and the corresponding genes belong to distinct biological pathways.
evidence: This is supported by functional analysis showing involvement in Wnt signaling, transcriptional regulation, translational regulation, and unknown pathways (Figure 4a and Results section).

claim: A broad mutational target size is the cause of P3.p's high mutational variance.
source: Our data indicate that a broad mutational target size is the cause of the high mutational variance and of the corresponding fast phenotypic evolutionary rate.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding of five different causal mutations in different genes without high mutation rates.

claim: A broad mutational target size is the cause of the fast phenotypic evolutionary rate of P3.p.
source: Our data indicate that a broad mutational target size is the cause of the high mutational variance and of the corresponding fast phenotypic evolutionary rate.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding of five different causal mutations in different genes without high mutation rates.

claim: Fast evolutionary change of a trait can be explained by the sustained action of natural selection acting in either a directional or a diversifying manner.
source: A possible explanation for fast evolutionary change of a trait is the sustained action of natural selection on the trait, acting in either a directional or a diversifying manner.
evidence: This is presented as established evolutionary theory.

claim: The available phenotypic variation onto which natural selection acts is not uniform along all axes of phenotypic space.
source: A second explanation arises from the fact that the available phenotypic variation onto which natural selection acts is not uniform along all axes of phenotypic space (developmental constraints or the 'arrival of the fittest') (Gould, 1977; Cheverud, 1984; Alberch and Gale, 1985; Maynard Smith et al., 1985; Arthur, 2004; Dichtel-Danjoy and Félix, 2004; Denver et al., 2005; Rifkin et al., 2005; Landry et al., 2007; Stoltzfus and Yampolsky, 2009; Wagner, 2014; Hether and Hohenlohe, 2014; McGuigan and Aw, 2017; Hine et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Upon random mutation, some axes of phenotype space are more readily explored than others.
source: Indeed, upon random mutation, some axes of phenotype space are more readily explored than others.
evidence: This follows from the previous claim about non-uniform phenotypic variation.

claim: The mutational variance may not be equal along different axes of phenotype space.
source: In other terms, the mutational variance may not be equal along different axes of phenotype space and this may sufficiently affect the rate of evolution at the phenotypic level.
evidence: This is a restatement of the concept of non-uniform phenotypic variation.

claim: Unequal mutational variance along different axes of phenotype space may sufficiently affect the rate of evolution at the phenotypic level.
source: In other terms, the mutational variance may not be equal along different axes of phenotype space and this may sufficiently affect the rate of evolution at the phenotypic level.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical possibility that the study aims to investigate.

claim: Short tandem repeats are more prone to spontaneous mutation.
source: some DNA sequences, such as short tandem repeats, are more prone to spontaneous mutation
evidence: This is supported by citations (Heale and Petes, 1995; Gemayel et al., 2010) mentioned later in the text.

claim: Short repeat regions in a gene may favour DNA replication slippage and recombination, leading to gain or loss of repeats.
source: Specifically, short repeat regions in a gene may favour DNA replication slippage and recombination, leading to gain or loss of repeats (Heale and Petes, 1995; Gemayel et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Short repeat regions may result in fragile DNA conformation susceptible to double-strand breaks.
source: or result in fragile DNA conformation susceptible to double-strand breaks (Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Highly mutable repeats may lie in a coding region.
source: Such highly mutable repeats may lie in a coding region (Verstrepen et al., 2005) or within regulatory sequences of a gene (Vinces et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Highly mutable repeats may lie within regulatory sequences of a gene.
source: Such highly mutable repeats may lie in a coding region (Verstrepen et al., 2005) or within regulatory sequences of a gene (Vinces et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Variation in highly mutable repeats has been shown to affect various phenotypes in different organisms.
source: Their variation has been shown to affect various phenotypes in different organisms (Levdansky et al., 2007; Undurraga et al., 2012; Gemayel et al., 2017; Dai and Holland, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Variation in highly mutable repeats in humans can lead to diseases such as Huntington and fragile X syndromes.
source: and in humans to lead to diseases such as Huntington and fragile X syndromes (Budworth and McMurray, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The high mutability of some DNA regions may accelerate the evolution of specific traits.
source: Consequently, the high mutability of some DNA regions may accelerate the evolution of specific traits.
evidence: This is presented as a logical consequence of the previous claims about highly mutable repeats.

claim: Dog head shape is a fast-evolving trait.
source: Examples are the fast-evolving dog head shape (Fondon and Garner, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Pelvic fin reduction in sticklebacks is recurrent.
source: or the recurrent pelvic fin reduction in sticklebacks (Chan et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The mutational variance increases with the number of genes whose mutation alters the phenotype.
source: the mutational variance increases with the number of genes (and size of gene regions) whose mutation alters the phenotype.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical principle.

claim: The mutational variance increases with the size of gene regions whose mutation alters the phenotype.
source: the mutational variance increases with the number of genes (and size of gene regions) whose mutation alters the phenotype.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical principle.

claim: Bacterial tolerance to antibiotics has frequent mutations because mutations affecting bacterial growth or lag time result in tolerance.
source: In another case, bacterial tolerance to antibiotics, mutations to tolerance are frequent because mutations affecting bacterial growth or lag time result in tolerance (Girgis et al., 2012; Girgis et al., 2009; Fridman et al., 2014; Brauner et al., 2016; Khare and Tavazoie, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Some traits are highly polygenic in natural populations.
source: Some traits are indeed known to be highly polygenic in natural populations.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge.

claim: An 'omnigenic' model proposes that phenotypic variation may result from variation at many genes outside the core pathways known to regulate the phenotype.
source: Some authors even proposed an 'omnigenic' model, where phenotypic variation may result from variation at many genes outside the core pathways known to regulate the phenotype (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The omnigenic model fits quantitative genetic data of human diseases.
source: This model fits quantitative genetic data of human diseases (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The nematode vulva relies on six precursor cells.
source: We use the nematode vulva to explore this question. This developmental system relies on six precursor cells
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The developmental fate of the six vulva precursor cells can be followed in a wide range of species.
source: (1) the developmental fate of the six homologous cells can be followed in a wide range of species
evidence: This is presented as an advantage of the system based on established knowledge.

claim: The mutational variance of different vulva precursor cells can be compared on the same scale.
source: (2) the mutational variance of the different precursor cells can be compared on the same scale
evidence: This is presented as an advantage of the system.

claim: Much knowledge has been accumulated on the specification of vulval precursor cell (VPC) fates through laser cell ablation studies and developmental genetics.
source: (3) much knowledge has been accumulated on the specification of vulval precursor cell (VPC) fates through laser cell ablation studies and developmental genetics.
evidence: This is presented as an advantage of the system based on the literature.

claim: The six vulva precursors are born aligned along the ventral epidermis of the young larvae and are numbered P3.p to P8.p from anterior to posterior.
source: The six vulva precursors are born aligned along the ventral epidermis of the young larvae and are numbered P3.p to P8.p from anterior to posterior (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The six vulva precursor cells initially share an identical fate of ventral epidermal blast cells.
source: The six cells initially share an identical fate of ventral epidermal blast cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Under the influence of several signalling pathways, each vulva precursor cell differentiates with a specific terminal fate.
source: Under the influence of several signalling pathways, each precursor cell differentiates with a specific terminal fate, creating reproducible patterns of cell fates shared by taxonomic groups of varying size (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The developmental fate of P3.p evolves faster than that of the other Pn.p cells, both within and among species in the Caenorhabditis genus.
source: As showed earlier, the developmental fate of one of these six cells, P3.p, by far evolves faster than that of the other Pn.p cells, both within and among species in the Caenorhabditis genus (Delattre and Félix, 2001; Kiontke et al., 2007; Braendle et al., 2010; Pénigault and Félix, 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: P5.p, P6.p and P7.p divide several times to form the vulva under the influence of EGF and Notch signaling.
source: While P5.p, P6.p and P7.p divide several times to form the vulva under the influence of EGF and Notch signaling
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: P4.p and P8.p most often divide once and their daughters fuse with the large epidermal syncytium hyp7 at the end of the third larval stage (L3).
source: P4.p and P8.p most often divide once and their daughters fuse with the large epidermal syncytium hyp7 at the end of the third larval stage (L3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The fate of P4.p and P8.p does not evolve in most of the Caenorhabditis genus.
source: Their fate does not evolve in most of the Caenorhabditis genus.
evidence: This is based on previous comparative studies.

claim: P3.p may either fuse to the hyp7 syncytium already at the end of the L2 stage or divide once in the L3 stage.
source: In contrast, P3.p may either fuse to the hyp7 syncytium already at the end of the L2 stage (with no further cell division possible) or divide once in the L3 stage (Sternberg, 2005; Félix, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: C. elegans and C. briggsae reproduce through selfing.
source: Isogenicity of the population is obtained easily in the two nematode species we use here, C. elegans and C. briggsae, because they reproduce through selfing (with the possibility of controlled outcrossing with males for genetic analysis).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these species.

claim: The particularly fast rate of phenotypic evolution of P3.p fate in the Caenorhabditis genus is very likely explained by its high mutational variance.
source: We previously showed using mutation accumulation (MA) lines that the particularly fast rate of phenotypic evolution of P3.p fate in the Caenorhabditis genus is very likely explained by its high mutational variance (Braendle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: When either C. elegans or C. briggsae wild isolates are subjected to spontaneous mutation accumulation, P3.p cell fate had the highest phenotypic variance compared with the other five cells.
source: Indeed, when either C. elegans or C. briggsae wild isolates are subjected to spontaneous mutation accumulation, P3.p cell fate had the highest phenotypic variance compared with the other five cells.
evidence: This is supported by data from Braendle et al., 2010 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: P4.p showed the second highest mutational variance and standing genetic variance, yet an order of magnitude lower than P3.p.
source: P4.p showed the second highest mutational variance and standing genetic variance, yet an order of magnitude lower than P3.p (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Braendle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and cited reference.

claim: The mutational variance of P3.p is an order of magnitude higher than that of P4.p and P8.p.
source: The mutational variance is here estimated by computing the per-generation change in mean frequencies of variant vulva patterns among MA lines, ΔV. ΔV is an order of magnitude higher for P3.p than for the other cells (10−5 vs 10−6, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Five MA lines were selected showing P3.p fate divergence with the ancestral line.
source: To this end, we selected five MA lines showing P3.p fate divergence with the ancestral line.
evidence: This is described in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: In each MA line studied, a single causal mutation was found.
source: In each line, we found a single causal mutation.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic mapping and validation experiments described in the Results.

claim: The five causal mutations are in five different genomic regions.
source: The five causal mutations are in five different genomic regions
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5a.

claim: The five causal mutations are not associated to highly mutable sequences.
source: are not associated to highly mutable sequences
evidence: This is supported by analysis in Figure 5 and comparison with mutation databases.

claim: The five causal mutations are different in nature (two SNPs, one small deletion and two large deletions).
source: and are different in nature (two SNPs, one small deletion and two large deletions).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Only one of the five causal mutations affected an expected gene involved in the Wnt pathway.
source: Functionally, only one of them affected an expected gene involved in the Wnt pathway, a 'core' signaling pathway known to regulate Pn.p fusion to the epidermis in the L2 stage (Pénigault and Félix, 2011b).
evidence: This refers to the sfrp-1 mutation, as described in the Results section.

claim: Two of the five causal loci encode general regulators of transcription and translation.
source: Two other loci encode general regulators of transcription and translation
evidence: This refers to cdk-8 and gcn-1, as described in the Results section.

claim: Two of the five causal loci lack functional annotation.
source: while the two final loci lack functional annotation.
evidence: This refers to R09F10.3 and Y75B8A.8, as described in the Results section.

claim: Fifteen MA lines derived from two C. briggsae and two C. elegans wild ancestors were selected that had accumulated mutations for 250 generations.
source: We selected fifteen MA lines derived from two C. briggsae (HK104 and PB800) and two C. elegans (PB306 and N2) wild ancestors that had accumulated mutations for 250 generations (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with a putatively deviant P3.p division frequency from a previous study (Braendle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: Six MA lines displayed large differences in P3.p division frequency compared to their corresponding ancestral line, ranging from 19% to 53%.
source: This led us to reduce the selection to six MA lines (two C. briggsae and four C. elegans lines) that displayed large differences in P3.p division frequency compared to their corresponding ancestral line, ranging from 19% to 53% (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b.

claim: 595 de novo mutations were listed in the six MA lines.
source: With this strategy, we listed 595 de novo mutations in the six MA lines, spread along the genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The 595 de novo mutations were mostly short indels (341), SNPs (250), and four large deletions.
source: These mutations were mostly short (i.e shorter than the 100 bp read length) indels (341), SNPs (250), and four large deletions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: All but one over 60 SNP tested were validated by direct re-sequencing.
source: We reliably used the SNPs from these calls directly as genetic markers: indeed, all but one over 60 SNP tested were validated by direct re-sequencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In all five MA lines studied, the phenotype segregated as a single locus.
source: In all cases, the phenotype segregated as a single locus.
evidence: This is based on the genetic mapping experiments described in the Results.

claim: The genetic intervals identified in the five MA lines ranged from 4 to 15 Mbp.
source: Serial backcrosses (once to four times) allowed to reduce the genetic interval, which still ranged from 4 to 15 Mbp (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic intervals were identified on four different chromosomes (I, III, IV and X) and two distinct regions on chromosome III.
source: Importantly, we identified intervals on four different chromosomes (I, III, IV and X) and two distinct regions on chromosome III.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genetic intervals were distinct in each MA line, excluding that recurrent mutations at a common locus could control the evolution of P3.p in the MA lines.
source: The genetic intervals were thus distinct in each line, excluding that recurrent mutations at a common locus could control the evolution of P3.p in the MA lines.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic mapping data.

claim: The molecular nature of the five mutations was diverse: two non-synonymous single-nucleotide substitutions, a small 16 bp deletion and two larger deletions of 1,344 bp and 54,355 bp.
source: The molecular nature of the five mutations was diverse (Figures 4a and 5a): two non-synonymous single-nucleotide substitutions, a small 16 bp deletion and two larger deletions of 1,344 bp and 54,355 bp.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4a and 5a.

claim: The two substitutions are a T-to-G transversion and a T-to-C transition, which are not the most frequent substitution types in Caenorhabditis spontaneous mutation accumulation lines.
source: The substitutions are a T-to-G transversion and a T-to-C transition, which are not the most frequent substitution types in Caenorhabditis spontaneous mutation accumulation lines (Denver et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data.

claim: The three-bp motifs (ATT and AGT) corresponding to the two substitutions were not reported to be those with the highest spontaneous mutation rates.
source: Considering the three-bp motif (with the mutant base at the 3' end) (Saxena et al., 2019), the corresponding motifs (ATT and AGT, respectively) were not reported to be those with the highest spontaneous mutation rates either.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data.

claim: Small deletions have lower mutation rates than single-nucleotide substitutions.
source: Small deletions have lower mutation rates than single-nucleotide substitutions (Saxena et al., 2019; Konrad et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Large deletions appear less frequent than large insertions/gene duplications.
source: As for the large deletions, they appear less frequent that large insertions/gene duplications (Konrad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The five mutations do not point to particularly frequent types of mutation.
source: Thus, these five mutations do not point to particularly frequent types of mutation.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of mutation types.

claim: The five causal mutations lie in regions with different GC contents (from 16% to 50% in a 50 bp window centered on the causal mutation).
source: they lie in regions with different GC contents (from 16% to 50% in a 50 bp window centered on the causal mutation)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The five causal mutations lie in regions either rich or poor in repeats.
source: in regions either rich or poor in repeats
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The five causal mutations lie in chromosome arms or centres.
source: in chromosome arms or centres (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a.

claim: 42% of mutations in C. elegans spontaneous MA lines were found in repeated sequences that represent 20% of the genome.
source: In sequence data of other C. elegans spontaneous MA lines (Saxena et al., 2019), we indeed found an overrepresentation of mutations in repeated sequences: 42% of mutations (n = 3469) were found in repeated sequences that represent 20% of the genome (X2-test: p-value<2.2×10−16; however, note that false-calling rates are expected to be higher in repeats).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published data.

claim: The two substitutions and the 16 bp deletion do not lie in repeats.
source: Of the causal mutations, the two substitutions and the 16 bp deletion do not lie in repeats.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 3' breakpoint of the large 54,355 bp deletion lies within a repeat.
source: The 3' breakpoint of the large 54,355 bp deletion lies within a repeat (Figure 5b)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The 3' breakpoint of the large 54,355 bp deletion is far away from the causative gene Y75B8A.8 that lies at the 5' end of this 54 kb deletion.
source: but is far away from the causative gene Y75B8A.8 that lies at the 5' end of this 54 kb deletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The large deletion in gcn-1 lies in an AT-rich region that may be classified as 'tandem and inverted repeats'.
source: The other large deletion, however, lies in an AT-rich region (two introns of the gcn-1 gene) that may be classified as 'tandem and inverted repeats'
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1j.

claim: The two breakpoints of the gcn-1 deletion correspond to a 20 bp direct repeat with two mismatches.
source: and the two breakpoints correspond to a 20 bp direct repeat with two mismatches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1j.

claim: No other mutation was found at the positions of the five causal mutations in 75 other MA lines.
source: We did not find any other mutation at the corresponding positions and the closest mutations were at least 4 kb away (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published MA line data.

claim: This result excludes an extremely high mutation rate at the position of the five causal mutations.
source: This result excludes an extremely high mutation rate at the position of the five causal mutations.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of recurrent mutations.

claim: None of the five nucleotide positions were mutated in the Million Mutation Project dataset.
source: None of the five nucleotide positions (breakpoints for deletions) were mutated in this dataset (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the MMP dataset.

claim: None of the five nucleotide positions were mutated in the C. elegans natural diversity dataset.
source: Second, we explored the C. elegans natural diversity (almost 3 million genomic variations from 766 wild strains; Cook et al., 2017), and none of the positions (the breakpoints for deletions) were mutated either (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the CeNDR dataset.

claim: The five identified mutations are not in mutational hotspots.
source: We thus conclude that the five identified mutations are not in mutational hotspots.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of multiple mutation datasets.

claim: gcn-1 is the 10th longest gene among the 21,803 C. elegans protein-coding genes.
source: Among the five genes, gcn-1 and to a lesser extent Y75B8A.8 stand out as large genes (measured from 5'UTR to 3'UTR, including introns): they are the 10th and 841st longest genes among the 21,803 C. elegans protein-coding genes, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Y75B8A.8 is the 841st longest gene among the 21,803 C. elegans protein-coding genes.
source: Among the five genes, gcn-1 and to a lesser extent Y75B8A.8 stand out as large genes (measured from 5'UTR to 3'UTR, including introns): they are the 10th and 841st longest genes among the 21,803 C. elegans protein-coding genes, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: None of the five genes showed a second hit in their exons in 75 C. elegans MA lines.
source: In the 75 C. elegans MA lines we analyzed, none of the five genes showed a second hit in their exons, even though some other genes were recurrently mutated, including in exons (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Genes accumulate mutations as predicted by their length in the MMP and CeNDR datasets.
source: In the MMP and CeNDR, genes accumulate mutations as predicted by their length (Figure 6b,c)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: gcn-1 retains natural variations at a higher rate than the average of genes, due to introns.
source: gcn-1 retains natural variations at a higher rate than the average of genes, due to introns, where variations are less likely to impact protein function (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The five causative genes do not present particularly high mutation rates given their length.
source: From these data, we concluded that the five causative genes do not present particularly high mutation rates given their length.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of mutation rates in different datasets.

claim: SFRP-1 is a highly conserved secreted Frizzled protein that inhibits Wnt signaling by sequestering Wnts.
source: SFRP-1 (Secreted Frizzled Receptor Protein-1, mutated in C. briggsae MA line 296) is a highly conserved secreted Frizzled protein that inhibits Wnt signaling by sequestering Wnts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SFRP-1 function.

claim: In C. elegans, the sfrp-1 gene is expressed in the anterior part of the nematode and the protein counter-acts the effect of posteriorly secreted Wnts.
source: In C. elegans, the sfrp-1 gene is expressed in the anterior part of the nematode and the protein counter-acts the effect of posteriorly secreted Wnts (Harterink et al., 2011; Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: P3.p is highly sensitive to the posterior Wnt gradient.
source: Since P3.p is highly sensitive to the posterior Wnt gradient (Pénigault and Félix, 2011b)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Loss of sfrp-1 should increase the frequency of P3.p division.
source: loss of sfrp-1 should increase the frequency of P3.p division.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known function of sfrp-1.

claim: An increase in P3.p division frequency was observed for C. briggsae MA line 296 and the corresponding sfrp-1 genome edits compared to the HK104 ancestor.
source: Indeed, we observed an increase in P3.p division frequency for C. briggsae MA line 296 and the corresponding sfrp-1 genome edits compared to the HK104 ancestor (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The effect of sfrp-1 on P3.p division is conserved in both C. elegans and C. briggsae.
source: Using an available null mutant line in C. elegans, we showed that the effect of sfrp-1 on P3.p division is conserved in both species
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The effect of sfrp-1 on P3.p division is opposite to the effect of a decrease in canonical Wnt signaling through a null bar-1 mutation.
source: and opposite to the effect of a decrease in canonical Wnt signaling through a null bar-1 mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The mutation in MA line 296 is a missense in the cystein-rich Frizzled domain that binds the Wnt ligand, changing a conserved asparagine into a histidine.
source: The mutation in MA line 296 is a missense in the cystein-rich Frizzled domain that binds the Wnt ligand, changing a conserved asparagine into a histidine (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The cdk-8 gene codes for a subunit of the Mediator complex.
source: The cdk-8 gene (cyclin-dependent kinase-8, mutated in C. elegans MA line 450) codes for a subunit of the Mediator complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cdk-8.

claim: The Mediator complex is a conserved eukaryotic multiprotein complex that interacts with chromatin, transcription factors and the RNA Polymerase II machinery and regulates the transcription of many genes.
source: This conserved eukaryotic multiprotein complex interacts with chromatin, transcription factors and the RNA Polymerase II machinery and regulates the transcription of many genes (Grants et al., 2015; Angeles-Albores and Sternberg, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In C. elegans, the CDK-8 module acts in a highly pleiotropic fashion.
source: In C. elegans, the CDK-8 module acts in a highly pleiotropic fashion yet a P3.p division frequency phenotype was not previously reported.
evidence: This is based on previous studies of CDK-8 function.

claim: A P3.p division frequency phenotype for the CDK-8 module was not previously reported.
source: In C. elegans, the CDK-8 module acts in a highly pleiotropic fashion yet a P3.p division frequency phenotype was not previously reported.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature.

claim: Mutation in three other genes encoding components of the CDK-8 module (cic-1, dpy-22/mdt-12 and let-19/mdt-13) also increased P3.p division frequency in an otherwise wild-type genetic background.
source: We found that mutation in three other genes encoding components of the CDK-8 module also increased P3.p division frequency in an otherwise wild-type genetic background (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c,d): cic-1, dpy-22/mdt-12 and let-19/mdt-13.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c,d.

claim: The valine-to-alanine substitution in the protein kinase domain found in MA line 450 likely causes a strong reduction-of-function.
source: The valine-to-alanine substitution in the protein kinase domain found in MA line 450 likely causes a strong reduction-of-function, since the phenotypes such as dumpy animals or P3.p division frequency were indistinguishable from those in animals bearing the null deletion allele cdk-8(tm1238) (Grants et al., 2016; Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a null allele, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: cdk-8 was not epistatic to bar-1, suggesting that CDK-8 functions independently of the Wnt signalling pathway.
source: The double mutants showed an intermediate level of P3.p division frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c), thus cdk-8 was not epistatic to bar-1 suggesting that CDK-8 functions independently of the Wnt signalling pathway.
evidence: This is based on epistasis analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The gcn-1 gene is a large protein of 2651 amino-acids including several Armadillo repeats, conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: The gcn-1 gene (homolog of yeast General Control Non-derepressible) is a large protein of 2651 amino-acids (aa) including several Armadillo repeats, conserved throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gcn-1.

claim: The GCN-1 protein is involved in translational control.
source: The GCN-1 protein is involved in translational control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GCN-1 function.

claim: GCN-1 promotes the phosphorylation of the eukaryotic initiation factor eIF2α.
source: GCN-1 promotes the phosphorylation of the eukaryotic initiation factor eIF2α (Nukazuka et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α is thought to globally repress translation while activating expression of a few specific genes in many eukaryotes.
source: which is thought to globally repress translation while activating expression of a few specific genes in many eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eIF2α function.

claim: The gcn-1 mutation in MA line 516 deletes the entire 21st exon and flanking intronic regions removing a part of the translation elongation factor three protein domain.
source: The gcn-1 mutation in the MA line 516 deletes the entire 21st exon and flanking intronic regions removing a part of the translation elongation factor three protein domain that is required for the efficient phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (Hirose and Horvitz, 2014).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and the cited reference.

claim: The MA line 516 gcn-1 mutation is likely a reduction-of-function allele.
source: From comparison with another partial deletion allele, gcn-1(nc40), the MA line mutation is likely a reduction-of-function allele (Figure 4—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This is based on comparison with another allele, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2e.

claim: GCN-1 had not been involved so far in the regulation of P3.p division.
source: GCN-1 had not been involved so far in the regulation of P3.p division.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature.

claim: Y75B8A.8 codes for a 715-aa protein lacking any known functional domain and homology outside nematodes.
source: Y75B8A.8, entirely deleted in MA line 418, codes for a 715-aa protein lacking any known functional domain and homology outside nematodes.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The Y75B8A.8 protein bears features of intrinsically disordered proteins, including polyglutamine stretches in the N-terminal half.
source: The protein bears features of intrinsically disordered proteins, including polyglutamine stretches in the N-terminal half (https://wormbase.org/species/c_elegans/protein/CE34135#065-−10).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis from WormBase.

claim: The homologous protein of Y75B8A.8 in the parasitic nematode Haemonchus contortus is found in excretory and secretory products and is able to bind the interleukin IL2 of its mammalian host.
source: The homologous protein in the parasitic nematode Haemonchus contortus is found in excretory and secretory products and is able to bind the interleukin IL2 of its mammalian host (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In C. elegans, the 3'UTR of Y75B8A.8 regulates RNA editing of the ADSR-2 mRNA.
source: In C. elegans, the 3'UTR of Y75B8A.8 regulates RNA editing of the ADSR-2 mRNA (Wheeler et al., 2015; Washburn and Hundley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Y75B8A.8 was not known to affect Pn.p cell development.
source: This gene was not known to affect Pn.p cell development.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature.

claim: R09F10.3 is a 468-aa protein with a weak similarity to the Mediator subunit MED27 at its C-terminus and no detectable similarity of the N-terminal part.
source: Finally, R09F10.3 is a 468-aa protein with a weak similarity to the Mediator subunit MED27 at its C-terminus and no detectable similarity of the N-terminal part (https://wormbase.org/species/c_elegans/protein/CE33810#065-−10).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis from WormBase.

claim: The short deletion in MA line 488 induces a frameshift and an early stop codon truncating more than 40% of the R09F10.3 protein length.
source: The short deletion in MA line 488 induces a frameshift and an early stop codon truncating more than 40% of the protein length.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: R09F10.3 was not known to affect Pn.p cell development.
source: This gene was not known to affect Pn.p cell development.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature.

claim: The higher mutational variance of P3.p cell division is not specifically due to the higher mutability of particular DNA sequences.
source: We conclude that the higher mutational variance of P3.p cell division is not specifically due to the higher mutability of particular DNA sequences and cannot be predicted from the genome sequence.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the analysis of the five causal mutations.

claim: The higher mutational variance of P3.p cell division cannot be predicted from the genome sequence.
source: We conclude that the higher mutational variance of P3.p cell division is not specifically due to the higher mutability of particular DNA sequences and cannot be predicted from the genome sequence.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the analysis of the five causal mutations.

claim: The higher mutational variance of P3.p cell division is a consequence of a broad mutational target impacting this cell fate specification.
source: Instead, it is a consequence of a broad mutational target impacting this cell fate specification, thus to the developmental context controlling the decision of P3.p to either fuse with hyp7 in the L2 stage or to further divide in the L3 stage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the analysis of the five causal mutations.

claim: At least three out of five identified mutations affected important fitness-related traits such as body morphology or fertility, as well as other vulva traits.
source: At least three out of five identified mutations affected important fitness-related traits such as body morphology or fertility, as well as other vulva traits (albeit at much lower frequency than changes observed for P3.p, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations documented in Supplementary file 6.

claim: P3.p is located at the fading end of the posterior-to-anterior Wnt gradient.
source: P3.p is located at the fading end of the posterior-to-anterior Wnt gradient
evidence: This is based on previous work cited (Pénigault and Félix, 2011b).

claim: P3.p may often receive a Wnt dose that is below the threshold required for its division, while P4.p and the most posterior cells are more robustly induced.
source: and may therefore often receive a Wnt dose that is below the threshold required for its division, while P4.p and the most posterior cells are more robustly induced.
evidence: This is an inference from the position of P3.p in the Wnt gradient.

claim: The sustained expression of the Hox gene lin-39 is required to prevent Pn.p cell fusion in the L2 stage.
source: In addition, the sustained expression of the Hox gene lin-39 is required to prevent Pn.p cell fusion in the L2 stage (Eisenmann and Kim, 2000), independently of Wnt signalling (Pénigault and Félix, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: P3.p is located at a very sensitive position that results in its developmental fate being highly sensitive to stochastic, environmental and genetic variation.
source: In summary, P3.p is located at a very sensitive position that results in its developmental fate being highly sensitive to stochastic, environmental and genetic variation (Braendle and Félix, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The broad mutational target found for P3.p is consistent with its developmental sensitivity.
source: The broad mutational target that we find here is consistent with this developmental sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the molecular findings to the developmental context.

claim: In the genus Oscheius, P3.p cell fate is not highly variable.
source: In another genus of the same family, Oscheius, P3.p cell fate is not highly variable (it does not divide)
evidence: This is based on previous comparative studies.

claim: In the genus Oscheius, P4.p and P8.p cell fates vary extensively both within and among species.
source: whereas P4.p and P8.p cell fates vary extensively both within and among species (Delattre and Félix, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.
